articles.title: Women's Rugby League World Cup - Australia 78-0 England: Poor English suffer humiliation
articles.summary: England are well beaten by defending champions Australia in their second Women's Rugby League World Cup Group A match in Perth.
articles.body:
Tries : Chapman 2, Kelleher 2, Church 2, Kelly 2, Robinson, Aiken, Kernick, Dodd, Weale, Penitani Gray, Bent Goals : Kelleher 9

After talk of lessons learned and improvements made, reality struck fast for England. They conceded a penalty just one second into their match against Australia - as Lucy Murray was two yards offside from kick-off.

It set the tone for another humiliating defeat, one which shows the gap to the Jillaroos has not shrunk since the thrashing in Las Vegas in March 2025.

On that occasion, England were 38-0 down at the break before losing 90-4. In Perth, Australia led 36-0 at the interval before winning 78-0.

England were not expected to beat World Cup co-hosts and reigning champions Australia in Group A. The Jillaroos have lost one international since 2016.

It is quite another thing for England to be as passive and error-prone as they were in this game, limp in the tackle and with questionable body language. Only six of this England squad were in Las Vegas, but quality-wise little has changed.

'We had to change after Vegas' - but England suffer another humbling

68-point swing and a Tonga win - how England avoid World Cup exit

After ceding advantage from the kick-off, England saw off the initial danger but were caught out chasing the kick from their try-line. Australia countered and Jaime Chapman scored.

England muffed the kick off for the second time in succession, straight out of play. Australia immediately attacked; after seven minutes, Chapman got up to take a high catch from Jocelyn Kelleher's kick and score.

After a brief flash where England thought they scored in the corner but Anna Davies' knee was in touch, they cheaply give the ball away and Tamika Upton broke two tackles before Kelleher crossed.

As Kelleher came round over the try-line to improve the position for the kick, wing Amelia Brown turned her back to play. It gave the impression England had already given up.

It was damage limitation for England, while the hosts could show off. After a score from Julia Robinson - who suffered a broken wrist shortly afterwards when being pinned by a team mate - Kelleher sliced in a swerving goal-kick of which Roberto Carlos would be proud.

Kelleher added her second try, and from the resulting kick off they attacked again, ending in Isabelle Kelly running over Fran Goldthorp.

Abbi Church crossed in the corner for 36-0. Soon after the restart, Australia went from one end to the other for Tarryn Aitken to bring up 40.

Olivia Kernick ran through three players in the non-existent defence to score, before Quincy Dodd forced over the 10th try under the posts.

Australia were in full showboat mode. Kelleher chip-kicked for herself before pinging an over-shoulder pass that led to Church's second try. The 12th try came as desperate England defence was not enough to stop Makenzie Weale.

The 13th came from Tiana Penitani Gray after a Brown knock-on, before Australia captain Kelly scored her second.

Shaylee Bent concluded the thumping, ending a move where multiple England tackles were shrugged off without blinking.

There was added pain for England as second row Eva Hunter exited with an ankle injury in the first half.

It adds to the loss of Jasmin Strange, who picked up a serious knee injury in training on Tuesday and was pitchside on crutches.

Goldthorp, England's best player on the night, carried on despite a nasty blow to her wrist.

As expected, England's qualification will come down to a decider against Samoa next Friday - where they must be better.

Matt's player of the match - Jocelyn Kelleher

One of the architects of Australia's extreme dominance might have been wearing England white had things panned out differently.

Jocelyn Kelleher, the New South Wales stand-off, qualified for England through parentage - but she showed no mercy for her mum's homeland as she and he athletic, skilful backs colleagues yielded try after try.

Kelleher's kicking game was precise, with a kick and chase chucked in for good measure, and her timing of pass helped her team-mates punch holes in their opponents.

England's loss is certainly Australia's gain.

articles.title: Japan 0-17 Wales - Visitors grind out scrappy WXV win in Tokyo
articles.summary: Wales earn a three-try victory against Japan in tricky Tokyo conditions to secure a second win of their WXV campaign.
articles.body:
Wales ground out a win over Japan in tricky Tokyo conditions to secure a second victory of their WXV campaign.

Swirling wind, rain and humidity made for a real battle between sides ranked 11th and 12th in the world, with a scrappy first-half looking likely to end scoreless.

But scrum-half Seren Lockwood's 35th-minute snipe gave the game a much-needed spark and the visitors a 7-0 advantage at the break.

Wales lost centre Freya Bell to a serious-looking knee injury, but the impact of the bench proved the difference as Kelsey Jones drove over off lineout ball, before Lockwood finished a rare moment of class at the death.

It was far from an impressive performance from Sean Lynn's resurgent Wales, but given their previous results, his side have now proven the ability to win ugly.

The two sides will meet again in Kumagaya City on Saturday, 31 October.

The hosts, who were playing in a double header with the men's side to celebrate Japanese rugby's centenary, had twice run Ireland close before their meeting with Wales.

But indiscipline has been somewhat of an Achilles heel, and they lost flanker Nami Asari to a yellow card just six minutes into the Test.

Wales looked to have taken immediate advantage from a five-metre lineout, with Jones peeling away to cross for what would have been her ninth international try, but on review, lock Jorja Aiono was deemed to have caused an obstruction.

Japan hit back with some attacking phases of their own, with Bell and Sisilia Tuipulotu combining well to hold prop Wako Kitano up over the line.

Wales continued to look comfortable in defence as Japan patiently went through the phases, but the visitors' renewed attacking prowess looked disjointed amid wayward kicks and handling errors.

It was disappointing considering Wales' 74-point haul in their previous two outings against South Africa and USA, but then conditions were not in their favour.

The breakthrough eventually came five minutes before the break, and it was again off a driving lineout.

The powerful Bell trucked the ball up to the line, with Lockwood quick to the breakdown and quick to spot a gap in the defence.

Bell added the conversion to end the half.

Japan came back out with much more attacking intent and looked more threatening as Wales began to slip off tackles.

Lynn's side were also dealt a blow when a distraught-looking Bell was stretchered off the pitch, but there was an able replacement waiting in Courtney Keight.

Lleucu George was also introduced before the hour mark as Wales looked to win back some territory, and the backline reshuffle paid off when they added a second try on a rare visit to Japan's 22 on 65 minutes.

And this time there was no denying Jones at the back of the driving maul, with Wales putting some distance between themselves and their hosts.

They looked to have added an immediate third try when Lockwood won the chase from Keira Bevan's hack through, but replays showed Jones' turnover in the build-up had been from an offside position.

Lockwood did, however, bag her second three minutes from time, with the makeshift wing finishing well after George's floating pass out wide.

Wales pushed for a try bonus-point with Nami Yoshida sin-binned, but had to settle for three to go with a first clean sheet since beating Hong Kong 65-0 in November 2018.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: How can England still qualify for the semi-finals? Scenarios to avoid historic group-stage exit
articles.summary: What do England need from Tonga and Samoa to reach the World Cup semi-finals? Group stage permutations and how England can avoid a shock early exit in Australia; England face Papua New Guinea in their final pool fixture on Friday (9.05am start)
articles.body:
A potential first group-stage exit in World Cup history became an increasing possibility after a heavy 30-12 defeat to Tonga in their tournament opener, with England still needing results to go in their favour even after an 82-0 demolition of France .

The unique format for this year's 10-team tournament sees the three teams in each of Group B and Group C feed into a combined six-team table, with only the top two sides then progressing to the semi-finals.

England currently have two points with one group stage match remaining, against Papua New Guinea on Friday (9.05am kick-off), where they will need another convincing victory to have any chance of progressing.

Head-to-head records will determine league positions over points difference, should multiple teams be tied, so qualification is now out of England's hands regardless of their own performance.

Tonga are already guaranteed to finish above England in the standings, having already picked up two wins this tournament and secured the better head-to-head record by beating them earlier this month.

England's hopes of progression rest on Tonga beating Samoa on November 1, which would see Kristian Woolf's side top the table on six points and see second spot decided on points difference.

Quite simply, before Tonga face Samoa, England must beat Papua New Guinea and do it by a considerable margin.

Samoa's thumping 78-4 win over France in their tournament opener and a 64-6 victory over Papua New Guinea on Saturday leaves them with an impressive +132 point difference.

England beating France takes them to a +64 points difference, 68 points behind Samoa heading into the final round of fixtures. Another win Friday would lift them to four points and level with both Samoa and Tonga.

McDermott's side would then be left to wait 48 hours for the outcome of Tonga vs Samoa in Sydney. A Samoa win would guarantee England's elimination, while a Tonga victory would see the points difference decide second spot.

England don't necessarily need to beat Papua New Guinea by 68 points or more, but a victory by that margin would mean any loss for Samoa would be enough to progress.

A smaller England win would see them need Samoa losing by a bigger score, depending on England's final points difference.

The winner of the combined Groups B+C table would progress to the semi-final to face the runner-up of Group A, a four-team league consisting of Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands.

Australia are favourites to top Group A after edging out New Zealand 24-22 in a thrilling tournament opener on October 15, with the winner of New Zealand vs Fiji on October 31 likely to take second spot.

The two semi-finals take place in Newcastle and Sydney respectively on November 7 and 8, with the Pool B+C winner in the opening semi-final, before the final takes place in Brisbane on November 15.

The format for the women's competition is less complicated, with eight teams separated into two pools of four and the top two from each then progressing to the semi-finals.

Samoa's 76-0 demolition of Wales leaves them level on points with England, who trail the Pacific islanders on points difference after their heavy 82-0 loss to Australia on Saturday.

England face Samoa in Wollongong on Friday, where the winners will confirm second in Group A with four points and book a semi-final meeting against the winner of Group B. An unlikely draw would see Samoa progress on points difference.

New Zealand - who have appeared in every Women's Rugby League World Cup final - are expected to top Group B, with Papua New Guinea, Fiji and France the others in that pool.

The two semi-finals are played on November 7 and 8 ahead of the final on November 15, with all three fixtures double-headers with men's matches. Australia are defending champions and chase a fourth consecutive World Cup title.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England coach Brian McDermott hails 'enormous' effort as France thrashing keeps semi-final hopes alive
articles.summary: England remain in World Cup semi-final contention after crushing win over France; another big victory against Papua New Guinea on Friday, coupled with a Tonga win over Samoa, could prove enough for England to reach semi-finals
articles.body:
England were left needing to win their two remaining pool matches by big margins, and for other results to go their way, after losing their opening fixture to Tonga last week.

They did all they could as they ran in 14 tries in a clinical display at Perth's HBF Park, with McDermott left to wonder what his side could have achieved with a longer build-up to the tournament.

McDermott said: "What we've done today, given the context, is just enormous.

"We had to win big but, as any coach will tell you, nobody thinks like that. You think, 'we've got to win'.

"We had some real good, candid conversations this week about what that actually means and we've been able to do that without getting distracted in chasing points.

"Everything was measured, everything was inside the game model, everything was what we planned to do - well, most of it at least.

"Whatever the results are next week, we want to finish strong against [Papua New Guinea] as well.

"If that means we're going home next Sunday night, that will be a big disappointment to us. But I'm not sure what more we could have done."

McDermott, who is new in the role, had limited preparation time with his squad and there were no warm-up fixtures.

"We've been together for five field sessions only," he said. "We're building something here and there was a little bit of that on show today.

"Certainly the tries we scored just before half-time are what we've been chasing. We can see how good that's going to be.

"If this group's together for a process or a long build-up to a tournament, we could achieve some special things but, over a short space of time, it's been remarkable really."

After a frustrating start, England took command with six tries, including three from Herbie Farnworth, in the latter stages of the first half.

Dom Young also finished with a hat-trick and AJ Brimson crowned a player-of-the-match display with the final try.

McDermott said: "We found our groove around about 25, 30 minutes, and then we scored a couple of tries, maybe three tries, back to back.

"But another pleasing factor is that when the game got tough, and we weren't allowed to score tries for fun, we buckled down and defended and worked hard. That's a really good sign."

articles.title: Ulster Rugby: Richie Murpyh's still without URC win after defeat by Bulls
articles.summary: Ulster's winless start to the United Rugby Championship stretches to four games as they are beaten 34-26 by the Bulls in Pretoria.
articles.body:
Tries: Coetzee 2, Louw, Grobbelaar Cons: Pollard 4 Pens: Pollard, Bosch

Tries: Mullins 2, McCann, McCloskey Cons: Murphy 3

Ulster's winless start to the United Rugby Championship stretched to four games as they were beaten 34-26 by the Bulls in Pretoria.

Former Ulster star Marcell Coetzee led the way for his side in a dominant pack effort, scoring two tries despite spending 10 minutes in the sin-bin.

From 21-0 down, the northern province did at least mount something of a comeback to secure a four-try bonus, although they were denied further consolation with Curwin Bosch's last-kick penalty knocking them out of losing bonus-point range.

While Richie Murphy's side did notch a Challenge Cup win against Zebre last week, it is the first time they have failed to win any of their first four league fixtures since 2008-09 when they opened what was then the Celtic League with a quartet of consecutive losses.

They face a second game in South Africa against Stormers on 31 October before the URC takes a four-weekend break for November's Nations Championship fixtures.

First-half struggles a familiar story for Ulster

In what was a clumsy start, Ulster conceded a penalty in the opening passage of play and were quickly made to pay when Coetzee finished off a maul try after only two minutes.

Turned over when given the opportunity to respond in kind, Ulster were soon defending their own line again but it took until the 19th minute for the Bulls to double their advantage, the hosts opting for the quick-tap when five metres out to set up an infield maul with Elrigh Louw dotting down.

With both the altitude and the bruising nature of the contest taking its toll on Ulster, Coetzee was over for his second and his side's third with a pick-and-go from close range eight minutes before the interval.

Seemingly hanging on and no more in the contest, Ulster scored their first points of the half with the clock in the red after working the ball well through the hands to send the speedy Chay Mullins over in the corner for his second try of the season.

Despite an uneven start to the campaign that now comprises of two draws and two losses in the league, spirited second halves have been a story of Ulster's season and they again were much brighter after the restart.

Mike Lowry thought he was over only to run out of room in the left corner but flanker David McCann barged across soon after.

Having been rocking on their heels in the first half, Jack Murphy's second conversion of the day left just seven points in it and Ulster's prospects improved further with Coetzee sent to the sin-bin after being shown a yellow card that stayed yellow when reviewed by the TMO bunker for a high hit.

By the time the former Springbok returned, it was his side who had scored the only points of his absence through a Handre Pollard penalty.

It was a further 10 minutes after the Bulls' captain's reintroduction before the game's next score with Keynan Knox doing well to create space for his team-mates to send Mullins over for his second.

Deflatingly for the visitors, virtually from the restart Johan Grobbelaar scored yet another forwards' try for the Bulls.

Stuart McCloskey, one of eight Ulster players who featured now joining up with Ireland for the Nations Championship, set up a grandstand finish with his side's fourth try 10 minutes from time.

They could not, however, close the gap in the final stages before Bosch's concluding penalty cost them a further point.

articles.title: WXV Global Series: South Africa 27-40 Ireland - Six-try Irish win in Cape Town
articles.summary: Ireland score six tries to beat South Africa in the first of two WXV Global Series meetings in Cape Town.
articles.body:
Tries: Hele, Ubisi, Tshiremba, Makua, Arries Con: Cilliers

Tries: Dalton, Djougang 2, Clohessy, Parsons, King Cons: O'Brien 5

Ireland scored six tries to mark their first trip to South Africa with victory over the Springboks in the first of two WXV Global Series meetings in Cape Town.

Aoife Dalton, Linda Djougang and Jane Clohessy crossed to give Ireland a slender half-time lead at the end of a ding-dong opening period in which Aseza Hele, Vainah Ubisi and Maria Tshiremba scored for the hosts.

Beibhinn Parsons and captain Erin King - who was sin-binned in the first half for a high tackle - extended Ireland's lead in the second half before Lerato Makua hit back for the Springboks.

But Djougang's second try put the result beyond doubt before Alichia Arries' late consolation score for the home side.

The sides meet again at Athlone Stadium on 31 October.

Wales grind out frustrating WXV win against Japan

Canada inflict back-to-back losses on England

Ireland and South Africa's only previous meeting was a 2006 Women's Rugby World Cup match in Canada, which the Irish won 37-0.

But it was clear from the opening exchanges in Cape Town that Saturday's contest would be a much closer encounter as the sides shared six tries in an entertaining first half, with Irish fly-half Dannah O'Brien's precision from the kicking tee proving the difference.

While Ireland were guilty of 13 handling errors, their line speed and multi-phase attack proved effective weapons against a spirited Springbok outfit.

Ireland struck first after seven minutes when Dalton showed impressive strength to burrow over the line from close range after Robyn O'Connor and Clohessy carries drove the visitors close to the posts.

But South Africa responded superbly and scored the pick of the tries when number eight Hele rampaged through the Irish defence for a fine individual score, with Ireland's early momentum further dented when King was sin-binned for a high tackle.

With King off the field, Ubisi scored to give South Africa the lead after 27 minutes before Djougang crashed her way over under the posts.

In an end-to-end conclusion to the half, winger Tshiremba thought she had given her side a half-time lead when she dotted down in the corner, but impressive second row Clohessy's effort - converted by O'Brien - was enough to edge the Irish in front.

Having been stunned by the United States' second-half comeback to lose in Dublin last month, Ireland quickly stretched their lead when scrum-half Emily Lane's neat offload sent prolific winger Parsons scampering through for her 26th international try within 90 seconds of the restart.

King then scored to atone for first-half indiscretion and when replacement scrum-half Aoibheann Reilly touched down, it appeared Ireland were home and hosed.

However, the try was ruled out for a knock-on by Brittany Hogan, and when Makua finished impressively after Ireland replacement centre Eve Higgins' yellow card, the Springboks dreamed of a late fightback with 12 minutes left.

But Djougang - again deployed as a loose-head prop having spent much of her career at tight-head - crossed for her second try to ensure an Irish win on South African soil before Arries' consolation effort two minutes from time.

Ireland, who lost their WXV opener to United States before beating Japan, will aim to close out the campaign with a third win from four games when they face the Springboks in Cape Town again on 31 October (13:00 GMT).

articles.title: Resurgent Leicester Tigers overpower Northampton Saints in derby downpour
articles.summary: Four second-half tries from Leicester defeat Northampton in a feisty wet weather contest.
articles.body:
Tries: Blamire, Henderson, Carnduff, Steward Cons: Searle Pens: Steward, Searle

Leicester Tigers gained revenge for their defeat in last season's Prem playoff semi-finals to defeat rivals Northampton Saints in torrential conditions at Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

In a first half played at the mercy of the weather, neither team was able to find a rhythm, with James Pater's early opportunist try and Freddie Steward's long-range penalty the only scores on the board.

But, inspired by a major scuffle on the verge of half-time, the Tigers subsequently dominated.

First, Jamie Blamire drove over from a rolling maul, before Cam Henderson barrelled his way through Saints tacklers to slide over in the corner.

Faced with the onslaught, the shellshocked Saints were unable to prevent further tries from Finn Carnduff and Steward, as the visitors' wait for a league win at their near rivals stretches to four years.

Van Poortvliet signs multi-year Leicester deal

Searle rejected France move to push on at Tigers

I'm serious about getting England call - Hendy

With the rain teeming down it was Saints who struck first. Playing with an advantage, Fin Smith's speculative kick ahead was spilled by Billy Searle allowing Pater to gather and score.

As the penalty count escalated amid the squall, neither team was able to keep the ball for long, but Freddie Steward gave the home fans something to shout about with a well judged penalty from 50 metres out.

Neither team was able to rely on their lineout, with Blamire suffering particularly at the hands of the marauding Josh Kemeny.

But with the whistle blown for half-time, the game's momentum shifted. A major scuffle involving multiple players broke out on the touchline, which eventually led to Ollie Chessum pushing England team-mate Henry Pollock down the tunnel.

Seemingly inspired by the tussle, the Tigers came out with a renewed purpose after the break.

Within minutes, Blamire was able to find his jumper five metres out and with the backs adding their weight, the Tigers powered over. The hooker ultimately emerging with the ball.

Having attained dominance in the scrum, the Tigers then struck again. Following strong running from Solomone Kata, Gabe Hamer-Webb and Henderson combined down the wing, to send the lock over the whitewash.

The Tigers were in the ascendancy and soon had a third through Carnduff, who drove over after a short-range pass from the imperious Joe Heyes as the Saints' defence tired.

Steward then put the gloss on the victory. The full-back stepping Archie McParland to grab what had appeared an unlikely try bonus point, to the delight of the home fans.

The result leaves the Tigers in second behind Gloucester, while Northampton drop to fourth.

Leicester Tigers' boss Geoff Parling told BBC Radio Leicester:

"I thought the players really took hold of [the game] in the second half. Some of the guys in the pack, the way we worked physically for each other – I'm really pleased.

"The set-piece didn't function early on. We were slow to adapt to the officiating there, but we got on the front foot and showed our power and application in that side of the game.

"The way that the players problem-solved at the set piece, which was an issue early, was brilliant and I'm just really pleased with the emotional energy that they threw into that game."

On being asked about the momentum switch at half-time:

"The changing room was honestly the calmest dressing room you could think of. We didn't have lots of tactical messages, we just felt we needed to be a bit more accurate and we'd gain the ascendancy."

Northampton boss Phil Dowson told BBC Radio Northampton:

"[In the second half] we didn't control that kicking game as well we had been. At the set piece the penalty count was very high – we didn't manage to produce enough ball, create enough pressure and we gave them lots of opportunities to score in our 22.

"They had the momentum throughout the second-half, our actions were neither accurate or aggressive enough and its cost us."

"A very bitter pill with that second half performance in particular."

On being asked about the impact of the weather:

"We play a winter sport and we have to get over that. We didn't work it out today and we need to be better at it [playing in the wet].

articles.title: United Rugby Championship: Glasgow recover 17-point deficit to beat Benetton
articles.summary: Glasgow recover from 17 points down to win a thriller at Benetton and continue their unbeaten start to the United Rugby Championship season.
articles.body:
Tries: Zanandrea, Lynagh Cons: Umaga 2 Pens: Umaga 2

Tries: Ferrie, Steyn, Darge, Oguntibeju Cons: Urwin, Kuenzle

Glasgow recovered from 17 points down to win a thriller at Benetton and continue their unbeaten start to the United Rugby Championship season.

The visitors went into half-time 10-0 down after a disappointing first-half display.

They squandered several attacking opportunities and were scythed open by Benetton fly-half Jacob Umaga, who released centre Federico Zanandrea for the game's first try.

Umaga also kicked a penalty before the break and when Louis Lynagh intercepted Matthew Urwin's pass to score under the posts on 42 minutes, Benetton appeared to be cruising to victory.

However, Glasgow responded in fine style, scoring three tries in eight minutes to level the scores.

Euan Ferrie went over off the back of a trademark rolling maul, captain Kyle Steyn crossed in the corner after some good hands and Rory Darge finished off a sweeping team move started by Steyn.

Umaga nudged Benetton back into the lead off the tee, but with time running out, lock Jare Oguntibeju crashed over from close range for Glasgow's fourth try.

It proved to be the decisive blow as Franco Smith's side navigated the final moments for a hard-fought win.

Warriors are second in the URC table, behind Edinburgh, after three wins and a draw, while Benetton sit 15th.

articles.title: WXV: Why winning ugly is just as important for Wales
articles.summary: It was far from a classic, but Wales' victory in Tokyo is another chapter in their transformation under Sean Lynn.
articles.body:
Wales set out their intention of returning to the world's top six before the start of their two Test series against Japan.

And while their 17-0 victory in Tokyo was far from a vintage showing, Wales have added an ability to win ugly to their armoury - something they are going to need if they are to once again dine at the very top table of women's rugby.

It was, of course, inspiring to see some of the Champagne rugby Wales produced in their eight-try mauling of South Africa in Cardiff last month, but grinding out a result and keeping a clean sheet on Japanese soil could prove to be just as important in Wales' transformation under Sean Lynn.

Prior to victory over the Springboks, Wales' previous Test success stretched back to the summer tour of Australia in 2025.

It was a long, frustrating and well-documented wait, but this group are finally starting to rack up some momentum, confidence and some all-important Ws.

Wales grind out frustrating WXV win against Japan

Wales earn hard-fought Japan win - as it happened

There had been a lot of excitment in the build-up in Japan, with both sides capable of producing an attractive brand of attacking rugby.

But conditions inside Tokyo's Prince Chichibu Memorial Stadium proved challenging for both sides, with wind, rain and 90% humidity.

It resulted in an 80-minute war of attrition and one Wales came out on top of thanks to a superior defence and being clinical on their few visits to Japan's 22.

"Coming away to Japan was always going to be tough," said Wales co-captain Kate Williams.

"I'm really proud of the way we dug in, stuck to our processes and in the second half we could show what we're really about.

"We problem solved and figured out other ways to get into the game."

There was very little between the two sides in the first hour, with Japan threatening to claw back their 7-0 half-time defecit.

Keira Bevan had slotted in at 10, but struggled to put Wales on the front foot with her kicking game.

Lynn instead introduced Lleucu George, with Bevan reverting back to scrum-half and Seren Lockwood moving out to the wing.

It was a reshuffle which paid off with George's boot putting Wales back in the right areas, and that coupled with the introduction of experienced forwards Gwenllian Pyrs, Bethan Lewis, Gwen Crabb and Georgia Evans proved the turning point in the match.

"Going in at 7-0 we knew there were areas that we needed to improve and I could see on the 53/54-minute mark that we needed some more territory.

"The girls, all 23 of the squad, were outstanding, and I thought the bench made a really big impact which was really good to see."

While the player of the match plaudits went to co-captain Williams, Lockwood's two -try dispay cements her status as one of Wales' most promising talents.

The 19-year-old, who was named 2026 Welsh Rugby Writers' Association women's young player of the year, started the game at nine, but looked equally comfortable out on the wing in the second-half.

A constant threat around the breakdown, her first-half snipe gave Wales a much-needed score before the break, while she showed pace and power to beat defenders for her second.

Lynn said before the game that next year's inaugural British and Irish Lions women's tour provided extra motivation for his players, and Lockwood has done her chances no harm whatsoever and could be considered as a potential bolter.

But Wales did lose another up and coming talent in centre Freya Bell, who had been at the heart of everything good Wales did in attack and defence.

She fell awkwardly in a tackle on 53 minutes before being carried off with a serious-looking knee injury. Lynn said she had gone for a scan with an update expected early next week.

Wales will play their final international fixture of 2026 on Saturday when they take on Japan again in Kumagaya City (07:00 GMT).

"I'm excited to come out for another round next week," said Williams.

"We're really evenly-fought teams and they are a tough opposition."

Wales started the year with a Six Nations wooden spoon, but following June's friendly victory over the Barbarians, could end the second half with a four wins from five.

It would be quite the turnaround from this time last year when Wales were still licking their wounds from a winless World Cup.

There was a feeling that all Lynn needed was time and he has now built a coaching group and squad with strength and depth, and one brimming with exciting young talent.

And with results now following, Wales are slowing starting to climb back up the rankings and back on world rugby's radar.

articles.title: Gallagher Prem: Leicester beat holders Northampton as Bristol get better of Exeter
articles.summary: Leicester Tigers' third win in four Gallagher Prem games - a 28-7 triumph over reigning champions Northampton Saints - takes them second in the table; Bristol Bears move third with hard-fought 20-7 victory over Exeter Chiefs in stormy conditions
articles.body:
Saints actually led at half-time at a soaking Mattioli Woods Welford Road, but they had no answer as the Tigers turned on the power to score four tries following the restart.

It meant that Leicester enjoyed a third win in four league games, as well as beating their East Midlands rivals at home for a fourth season running, in jumping up to second in the table.

The wet and windy conditions quickly played a part as Northampton grabbed the game's opening try after only seven minutes. With advantage being played, Fin Smith chipped towards the Leicester try line and, after Billy Searle's fumble, James Pater pounced to score, with Smith adding the conversion.

The Tigers were on the board after 19 minutes when Freddie Steward blasted a superbly struck penalty between the uprights from just inside the Northampton half.

It remained 7-3 to Saints at half-time, but a fracas down the touchline as the players made their way towards the tunnel indicated a fiery second half was on the way.

The home crowd was brought to its feet four minutes after the restart when a driving maul rumbled its way over with Jamie Blamire grounding the ball, although Searle's missed conversion meant Leicester's lead was just one point.

But their dominant start to the half brought a second try when the ball was worked out to the left to Gabriel Hamer-Webb whose pass led to Cameron Henderson scoring in the corner. Searle's conversion again slid wide.

The Tigers were more than a score clear, though, when Finn Carnduff crashed over from close range in the 57th minute after a beleaguered Saints defence had illegally collapsed a maul.

Having not converted any of his side's three tries to that point, Searle extended the hosts' lead further with a penalty from in front of the posts.

Northampton's afternoon continued to disintegrate when they had Tom Lockett sin-binned for making head-on-head contact with Solomone Kata with 10 minutes left.

And the Tigers rubbed their noses in it by claiming a bonus point not long after when Searle's long pass found Steward and the England full-back glided in under the posts.

Bristol see off Exeter in stormy conditions to move third

Bristol Bears moved third in the table with a hard-fought 20-7 win over Exeter Chiefs in appalling conditions at Ashton Gate.

It was their fifth successive league victory over Rob Baxter's men after an old-style-rugby war of attrition in heavy rain and strong winds.

Exeter had the better of the opening exchanges and enjoyed a period of pressure on the home line. However, hanging on to the slippery ball in the tackle was proving a major problem for the visitors and several potential scoring opportunities were squandered.

Even though they had their own difficulties, Bristol's handling was much better and it enabled them to put a lot of pressure on the Exeter line, but the Chiefs' defence held firm.

It looked likely that the interval might be reached with the game still scoreless until a long pass by England scrum-half Harry Randall found Gabriel Ibitoye in space on the left wing, and he made light of the attempted cover tackles to cross in the corner and give the Bears a 5-0 lead.

Centre James Williams slotted an excellent touchline conversion and he was also on target with a 35-metre penalty three minutes later, when Olly Woodburn was penalised for not releasing in the tackle after catching one of many high balls he had to deal with in the first half, to increase the Bears' lead to double figures.

Chiefs had a chance to break their duck nine minutes into the second half when Henry Slade tried to get on the end of Sam Wolstenholme's grubber kick through the home defence, but the ball squirmed from his grasp.

Moments later, though, Chiefs kicked a penalty to the corner and Greg Fisilau was driven over in emphatic style, with Slade converting to get the Chiefs right back in the contest.

They even had chances to draw level in the last 10 minutes when they turned down two kickable penalties inside the 22, but when Bristol got their own opportunity three minutes from time, Williams was immaculate with the boot.

And when Luka Ivanishvili forced his way over moments later, the win was sealed and Chiefs were denied the losing bonus point.

articles.title: Leinster 24-18 Munster: Leinster fight back to beat Irish rivals in bruising URC derby
articles.summary: Leinster fight back to secure a bonus-point win over Munster in a bruising United Rugby Championship derby at Aviva Stadium.
articles.body:
Tries: T O'Brien, Baird, Tector, Osborne Cons: Carbery 2

Tries: Daly, O'Connor Con: O'Shea Pens: O'Shea 2

Leinster fought back to secure a bonus-point win over Munster in a bruising United Rugby Championship derby at Aviva Stadium.

A year on from a stirring win over their rivals at Croke Park, Munster raced into a 13-0 lead through Shane Daly's try and eight points from the boot of 20-year-old fly-half Charlie O'Shea.

However, Tommy O'Brien hit back for Leinster before half-time after being set up by fit-again scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park, who notched three try assists in an eye-catching display.

Ryan Baird and Charlie Tector's second-half tries edged an increasingly dominant Leinster in front before Jamie Osborne's late score secured the home side's bonus point.

Having been held scoreless since the 29th minute, full-back Ben O'Connor crossed in the final minute to secure a losing bonus point for Munster.

While the two sides' internationals prepare to enter Ireland camp before November's Nations Championship fixtures, Leinster travel to Connacht in another interprovincial fixture on Friday (19:45 GMT) before Munster welcome the Sharks to Thomond Park on Saturday (17:30).

Ulster still without URC win after defeat by Bulls

Scarlets denied by Stormers in 14-try thriller

As ever when these fierce rivals lock horns, there was a plethora of intriguing sub-plots, from hooker Dan Sheehan's surprise switch to number eight to Munster's first outing since only two of their players made the latest Ireland squad.

But similarly to last year's Croke Park tussle, Munster looked fired up from the start and edged ahead through O'Shea's penalty after James Ryan's high tackle on Kieran Brookes.

Finding both set-piece and breakdown joy, Munster scented blood and scored the game's opening try when O'Shea, Sean O'Brien and Craig Casey combined in flowing fashion to put Daly through.

Intent on maintaining scoreboard pressure, O'Shea stretched the away side's lead with a wind-assisted penalty from just inside his own half after Alex Nankivell forced a turnover.

Leinster needed a surge of inspiration before half-time, and returning playmaker Jamison Gibson-Park - one of 11 British and Irish Lions in their starting line-up - delivered.

Following a Leinster scrum five metres out from the Munster line, the Ireland scrum-half flung an inch-perfect pass out to right winger O'Brien, who skipped past Ben O'Connor to score.

There was controversy when Munster back row Gavin Coombes alleged he was grabbed in the groin by a Leinster player.

After consulting with the television match official (TMO), referee Andrew Brace told Munster captain Tadhg Beirne there was no conclusive footage to review, although the incident could be referred to the citing commissioner.

Early in the second half, momentum shifted when a penalty awarded to Munster was reversed following a late tackle by Brookes.

From there, Leinster kicked into Munster territory and left with a converted try nearly 10 minutes later when Baird forced his way over the line after a spell of sustained pressure, with Nankivell sin-binned following a string of Munster infringements in the build-up.

Joey Carbery, deputising for the injured Sam Prendergast in his first start since returning to Leinster, converted to bring the hosts to within a point.

With Nankivell off the field, Leinster pounced on a missed Munster line-out to launch an attack that culminated with Gibson-Park teeing up Tector to give the home side the lead for the first time with 16 minutes left.

After a lengthy stoppage following a serious injury sustained by Daly, Leinster went hunting for the bonus-point score and found it when Gibson-Park sent Osborne through eight minutes from time.

O'Connor's late score ensured Munster did not leave Dublin empty-handed, but given their early ascendancy, it proved a disappointing night as Leinster's persistence and big-game prowess told.

articles.title: Ospreys 31-14 Dragons: Swansea side return to St Helen's in style in URC
articles.summary: Ospreys do the double over Dragons in the United Rugby Championship in their winning return to St Helen's.
articles.body:
Tries: Morgan-Williams 2, Parry, penalty try, Moriarty Cons: Edwards, Morgan-Williams

Ospreys enjoyed a happy homecoming with a bonus-point victory over Dragons at St Helen's.

Mark Jones' side returned to the famous Swansea venue in style, scoring five tries in horrendous conditions in front of 5,592 supporters.

Ospreys led 19-7 at half-time after a double by Reuben Morgan-Williams and an effort by captain Sam Parry.

Dragons scored with the final play of the half through Rio Dyer, but Ospreys' driving line-out secured the win by earning a penalty try and a score for Ross Moriarty.

Anzelo Tuitavuki went over for the visitors' second, but they endured an evening to forget.

Dragons had Rhodri Williams, Tinus de Beer and Aneurin Owen sin-binned and Wales were also given a scare before the Nations Championship.

Dyer did not come out for the second half and lock Ben Carter, who established himself in Steve Tandy's starting line-up last season, went off with a head injury.

After some pre-match pomp, Ospreys started strongly and got their reward when scrum-half Morgan-Williams burrowed over from close range in the sixth minute, Dan Edwards adding the extras.

The visitors did a good job of playing into the wind and had been the better side, but then conceded a scrappy second on the half hour.

Morgan-Williams was the beneficiary of Dragons' failure to fall on the ball after a grubber through by centre Lalakai Foketi.

Ospreys were over for a third time as half-time approached when fly-half Edwards was brave with a penalty touch-finder and the pack muscled over from a five-metre driving line-out for Parry's score.

A 19-0 lead would have represented a good effort for Ospreys with the wind, but Dragons had the final say of the half when, after pressure and penalties, recalled Wales wing Dyer crossed for his first try of the season.

A new old home for Ospreys side fighting for a future

Scarlets denied by Stormers in 14-try thriller

Wales great Faletau suffers fresh injury blow

Those seven points were cancelled out almost straight from the restart when Ospreys were awarded a penalty try for a 20-metre line-out drive being stopped illegally, with scrum-half Rhodri Williams sin-binned.

Dragons then suffered the loss of co-captain Carter and, straight after Williams' return, a yellow card for De Beer.

Edwards pinned them into the corner from the resulting penalty and the pack did the rest, back-row forward Moriarty following Parry in scoring against his former side.

Tuitavuki gave Dragons a smidgen of hope when he sniped at a ruck and powered over with quarter of an hour left, but that was soon followed by Owen's yellow card for a head-on-head tackle.

After a first block of the season that has seen Ospreys play in Durban, Johannesburg, Tbilisi and Newport, they returned to the famous sporting venue they left in 2005.

They have downsized after leaving the Swansea.com Stadium in 2025 and, while there is a long snagging list and plenty of jobs to be done, this felt like a home.

Like at Bridgend's Brewery Field, their ground for 2025-26, there was a lively atmosphere to make up for the rough edges.

It was Ospreys' first game at St Helen's since moving a game against Benetton during the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Their return meant there were plenty of smiles despite torrential rain, especially from the punter who conquered the conditions to win a new £20,000 bathroom by passing the ball through a hole at half-time.

Ospreys came out firing after the restart to ensure that their first half efforts did not go down the pan on a night to remember for the region as they continue to fight for their existence.

articles.title: United Rugby Championship: Ulster head coach Richie Murphy praises team for 'sticking in the fight' against Bulls
articles.summary: Ulster head coach Richie Murphy praises his team for their battling qualities and execution of their gameplan which almost saw them earn a comeback win against the Bulls in Pretoria.
articles.body:
Ulster head coach Richie Murphy praised his side's fighting qualities as they battled back from a 21-point deficit against a dominant Bulls to go close to securing an upset against the South African side in Pretoria.

In the end, the hosts ran out 34-26 victors against the Irish province in the United Rugby Championship encounter at Loftus Versfield Stadium.

Ulster came away with a bonus point for scoring four tries but were denied a second bonus point by Curwin Bosch's penalty with the last kick of the game.

Former Ulster star Marcell Coetzee led the way for his side in a dominant pack effort, scoring two of his side's four tries despite spending 10 minutes in the sin-bin.

Ulster are still without a win in their URC campaign, having drawn two and lost two of their league matches this season.

"We struggled at the start to get a foothold in the game. Our first three possessions were probably turned over too easily and that puts you under pressure, especially when you're playing against a team like the Bulls," Murphy reflected after the game.

"They got access into our '22' and coming up to half-time they had about 65% territory and possession.

"I thought our guys did a really good job of sticking to the plan, executing and having a chance two or three plays to go to actually win the game.

"So we were disappointed in the end and disappointed to give up the bonus point in that last play of the game."

'Plenty of teams come here and roll over'

Murphy lamented his team's indiscipline in the first half, highlighting that as a contributory factor in leaving them with a mountain to climb.

"Our scrum held up reasonably well. Everyone knows when you come to South Africa your scrum is going to be under pressure so it's an area we need to get better at.

"We had a way we wanted to play. We probably went away from that early on in the game but we got more towards what we were trying to do towards the back end of the half and in the second half.

"You have to stick in the fight here. Plenty of teams come here and kind of roll over.

"I don't think we did that, which I'm really proud about, the way the lads stuck to the task."

A Stuart McCloskey pass looked to have set James McKillop galloping clear on the wing to put Ulster in with a chance of what at one stage appeared a very unlikely victory but the Ireland centre was adjudged to have had part of his foot in touch.

"Stu's foot was probably just in touch but if he gets that away earlier we're going into the last two minutes with a lead. But that's the breaks," bemoaned the Ulster coach.

Murphy highlighted the breakdown as another area his side could improve on before next week's meeting with the Stormers in Cape Town.

"We have to learn lessons but we will benefit from these tight battles come the end of the season," he added.

The province's Ireland internationals will return home to join up with Andy Farrell's international squad, which assembles on Monday, while Murphy revealed that seven squad reinforcements would be arriving in Cape Town to bolster his side's ranks ahead of the game with Stormers.

articles.title: Ospreys enjoy happy St Helen's return as Dragons, Scarlets and Cardiff lose in URC
articles.summary: The Welsh URC talking points as Ospreys win their St Helen's homecoming, Scarlets give Stormers a scare and Cardiff and Dragons disappoint.
articles.body:
With three wins in a row and back at their St Helen's home, Ospreys are Wales' buoyant side with one round to play in the first block of the season.

Mark Jones' side completed a United Rugby Championship (URC) double over the Dragons with a strong performance in the wind and rain on Saturday.

Seventh in the table, and their South Africa double-header played, Ospreys will be in good shape if they can enjoy another derby win against Cardiff before the break for the Nations Championship.

The Blue and Blacks have plenty to consider after being overpowered by Sharks at the Arms Park, while Scarlets showed signs of their improvement despite being on the wrong end of a thriller at Stormers.

Ospreys thump Dragons on return to St Helen's

Scarlets denied by Stormers in 14-try thriller

There will be relief and pride in Swansea after the Ospreys' successful St Helen's homecoming.

The 24 October return to the famous ground - still undergoing redevelopment - looked ambitious when the URC fixture list was announced.

But Ospreys delivered off the field despite the horrendous weather, and then on it in front of 5,592 supporters against Dragons.

"There was a lot of pressure on the boys around the whole occasion. You only get one chance to make a first impression," said head coach Jones.

"It was a proper Ospreys performance and it needed to be in those conditions.

"It wasn't just a win, it was a really good performance because there was a lot of high-quality skill in there, some good defensive work and our set-piece shone through. The effort was class."

Those looking for faults at the revamped home would have been nit-picking.

A remarkable amount of work has already gone into the makeover in a short space of time and there is still plenty to do as Ospreys steadily improve the facility.

"I played here growing up in finals, with schools and playing for Swansea as well," said Wales wing Keelan Giles.

"I'd never played in front of a crowd that big here. It was a great night, a great experience and it's class to be here again.

"They've done an amazing job and the atmosphere was top notch."

More jobs will be ticked off in the coming week for the visit of Cardiff, when a win would put Ospreys in good shape given the travel demands of the first block.

Ospreys will face Cardiff without Wales scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams, who is in pole position to be Tomos Williams' deputy in the Nations Championship.

He signed off with a double against Dragons and joined forces with Dan Edwards to guide the side around in tricky conditions.

The 28-year-old has had to be patient with Wales but looks set for a chance in November, in part due to the injury of Ospreys team-mate Kieran Hardy.

Jones said: "He's definitely earned the opportunity. I love how honest he is around his work and he always wants to get better.

"He is an Ospreys through and through, a Neath boy who loves the badge, loves coming to work and is so consistent.

"He's got that sort of dour face and you never know if he's excited or annoyed! But he is always the same and consistent."

Morgan-Williams, who won his third cap off the bench against South Africa in the summer, is joined in the squad by Dragons prospect Che Hope.

"Tomos is locked in at number one with Wales at the moment but Reubs has done a class job for us," said Jones.

"If he is called upon by Wales then he will do an awesome job. I couldn't think of a better guy to be in that squad to help Wales."

Scarlets showed tenacity and courage at Stormers to go along with their attacking verve, but might just feel it was an opportunity missed in Cape Town.

A solitary try bonus did not seem a fair reflection of their effort when trading blows with a URC heavyweight.

After a disheartening opening fortnight when beaten by Cardiff and Dragons, Scarlets look in far better shape thanks to playing at pace and adding the direct running of fit-again number eight Fletcher Anderson to their guile.

They made 21 clean breaks and beat 42 defenders against Stormers, and that without chief game-breaker Blair Murray prior to his November with Wales.

"You can't come here and admire the way the Stormers play, you have got to come here and challenge them and dare to be great," said director of rugby Nigel Davies.

Teenage fly-half Carwyn Leggatt-Jones pulled the strings superbly and centre Joe Roberts continued his strong start to the season with a hat-trick.

But Scarlets lost their losing bonus point in the closing stages when trying to earn a draw and three points.

They also failed to edge in front after getting to 40-40 against a Stormers side whose injuries had left them without a specialist hooker to throw in and were deprived of their dominant scrum.

There will be regrets - and defence coach Eamon O'Carroll has plenty of work to do after his arrival from St Helens - but another opportunity comes this Saturday at Bulls.

Scarlets will attempt to cause an upset without in-form wing Macs Page , who was given oxygen while leaving the field after heavily hitting the floor with his head when trying to score a second try.

Wales great Faletau suffers fresh injury blow

Cardiff were outplayed in all departments by Sharks on Friday, with the South Africans becoming the first away side to win at the Arms Park in 2026.

The Blue and Blacks can point to a farcical five-day turnaround from their Champions Cup defeat by Northampton - Saints boss Phil Dowson labelled it "nuts" - but there will be frustration at the manner of the defeat.

They turned around a half-time deficit and had the wind at their backs, yet spent the final quarter pinned deep inside their own half.

Cardiff failed to earn at least one match point just once last season - at Glasgow - but have already fired two blanks in the current campaign against Leinster and Sharks.

That ramps the pressure up for a derby at Ospreys as Cornel van Zyl's side attempt to make the play-offs for the second successive year.

They will travel west without James Botham, who will be with Wales as he attempts to earn a spot against Japan.

All of Tandy's back-row forwards put in prominent performances but Botham showed his qualities against a powerful side when scoring two tries, making 27 tackles and winning three turnovers.

"Jim is a tough character who works hard, is athletic and robust. He stood up to the challenge," said Van Zyl.

Botham came off the bench against Fiji and South Africa in the summer, either side of a start versus Argentina.

Dragons have been doubled by Ospreys and this time there were few positives to take from the defeat.

"We're so much better than what we showed. We were second best in most things," said head coach Filo Tiatia.

Dragons must lick their wounds and get ready for a banana skin against Zebre.

They also suffer the impact of missing a six-strong Wales contingent to add to their lengthy injury list.

Dragons will hope that Harri Keddie and Thomas Young can boost the back row, leaving them to worry about second row and midfield.

They are without locks Ben Carter, Seb Davies and Levi Douglas and it is feared Tonga centre Fetuli Paea suffered a serious injury in the closing stages in Swansea, with Tiatia already without Aneurin Owen and Harri Ackerman.

Dragons needed to cash in on a favourable first block and a bonus-point win against Zebre would take them to a steady 14 points along with a Challenge Cup win against Perpignan.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Australia reach World Cup semis & New Zealand get back on track
articles.summary: Australia edge to a 36-22 victory in a pulsating Group A match against Fiji to book their place in the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.
articles.body:
Australia edged to a 36-22 victory in a pulsating match against Fiji to book their place in the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.

Having lost their previous five meetings against Australia by an aggregate score of 246-16, a stunned Brisbane crowd watched Fiji enjoy territorial advantage in the first half and take a 16-12 lead after the break.

However, the momentum switched back to Kevin Walters' side in a crucial 60-second spell.

Solomone Saukuru raced in to seemingly put Fiji 20-12 ahead - but when it was ruled out for obstruction, Australia immediately went up the other end and Tom Trbojevic scored to bring the teams level.

Trbojevic, who looked vulnerable in defence, crossed twice more for Australia and Jacob Preston added a further try after Semi Valemei had completed his hat-trick for Fiji.

"There are definitely some areas to improve on," Trbojevic told Premier Sports. "We didn't start as we wanted to and couldn't get a flow. We just needed to play our style of footy.

"We weren't at our best but we came away with two points. We need to improve. We've got to enjoy a win but we've got to be our harshest critics too."

Brisbane Broncos centre Kotoni Staggs had opened the scoring for Australia on his home ground, while Sam Walker capped his debut with a try and 12 points with the boot.

But the manner in which their pack were outmuscled - and in which they allowed Taane Milne and Valemei to score - will be a concern for Walters, whose team head into the last four despite delivering two unconvincing performances in beating New Zealand and Fiji.

New Zealand will take on Fiji in a make-or-break final pool game on Saturday, 31 October (04:30 GMT), having overcome an early scare themselves in their 82-16 victory over the Cook Islands in Christchurch.

Jamayne Isaako, who is joining Melbourne Storm next term, took the headlines as he scored a record 38 points for the Kiwis.

It was the perfect way for Stacey Jones' team to bounce back from their 24-22 opening Group A defeat by Australia but it did not go entirely to script, as the Cook Islands recovered from 12-0 down to lead 16-12.

With two-time World Cup winner Valentine Holmes in their ranks, Karmichael Hunt's team responded superbly as Esom Ioka grabbed a hat-trick of tries in response to early efforts from Isaako and Ronaldo Mulitalo.

However, from there it was one-way traffic as the Kiwis took control to lead 36-16 by the break.

Isaako crossed three times overall, while Test debutant Tanner Stowers-Smith, Mulitalo and Casey McLean each scored twice.

Scott Sorensen, Kodi Nikorima, Te Maire Martin, Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad and Keano Kini, who replaced injured star full-back Kalyn Ponga in the New Zealand line-up, also claimed tries.

Isaako's points haul - which included 13 conversions - eclipsed Tasesa Lavea's previous mark of 32 points in a single game, which was recorded against the same opposition in 2000.

Kiwi Ferns roll towards Samoa or England clash

New Zealand's women had earlier thrashed France 92-0 in the same stadium, with Apii Nicholls scoring four tries.

Stacey Waaka and Mele Hufanga both claimed a hat-trick of tries in a dominant performance by the co-hosts.

Mackenzie Wiki, Raecene McGregor and Tenika Willison all crossed twice with Chantay Kiria-Ratu and Kaiyah Atai also going over in an 18-try demolition job.

The Kiwi Ferns have now defeated France by a combined score of 236-0 across three World Cup encounters.

New Zealand, who defeated Fiji 18-12 in the their opening match, will round off their Pool B campaign against Papua New Guinea on Saturday, 31 October (06:45 GMT).

Ricky Henry's side look set to face either Samoa or England in the semi-finals of the competition.

Fiji face France in the other remaining group match on Saturday, 31 October (02:20 GMT).

articles.title: Leinster 24-18 Munster: Clayton McMillan backs Gavin Coombes after alleged groin grab incident
articles.summary: Munster head coach Clayton McMillan backs Gavin Coombes after the back row alleged he had been grabbed in the groin in Saturday's defeat by Leinster.
articles.body:
Munster head coach Clayton McMillan has backed Gavin Coombes after the number eight alleged he had been grabbed in the groin during Saturday's 24-18 defeat by Leinster.

Coombes alleged the incident happened with an unnamed Leinster player at a ruck towards the end of the first half of the United Rugby Championship derby at the Aviva Stadium.

Coombes raised the allegation with match referee Andrew Brace, but the television match official (TMO), Colin Stanley, could not find any video evidence of the incident.

Speaking after the game, McMillan backed Coombes and, referencing the citing commissioner who can punish retrospective incidents after a review, said it was something that had to be left "for the powers that be".

"All I know is that I back our players 100% that if they make an allegation like that, they wouldn't do it lightly," McMillan said.

"He's not that sort of person, Gavin, so we'll see where that goes."

Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said he did not see the incident but said it was a "serious matter" for the citing commissioner.

Cullen also said it "looked like he [Coombes] changed his mind halfway through the accusation".

"That's the way it sounded, once the scrum was packing down," said Cullen.

"But I don't know. Obviously, once that accusation is made, it becomes a serious matter for the citing commissioner.

"My comment is not going to help in any way here, but from what I've seen, I can't see anything."

articles.title: Harlequins 33-15 Saracens: Marcus Smith stars on 200th appearance as Quins seal first Gallagher PREM win of season
articles.summary: Marcus Smith stars on landmark appearance as Harlequins win for the first time in this season's Prem; "Hopefully that can kick-start our Prem season," fly-half says after early try sets Quins on way to victory
articles.body:
It was the hosts' first victory of the Gallagher PREM season, with Quins running in three first-half tries and a penalty try against their London rivals at The Stoop.

Fly-half Smith, who made his senior debut for Harlequins during the 2017-18 season at the age of 18, touched down within three minutes of kick-off in his milestone match to score the fastest try of the season so far.

"Obviously, to get our first win of the season today, of all days, off the back of a storm, I was nervous coming out with the wind," Smith told TNT Sports .

"Hopefully that can kick-start our Prem season."

Quins showcased some exceptional heads-up rugby, with Fin Baxter popping off a one-handed offload to Seb Driscoll for the hosts' second try of the match.

Though Saracens were ill-disciplined, they threatened Quins on multiple occasions, with Rotimi Segun dancing around three defenders on his way to the try line for the visitors' first score.

But Quins hit back, mauling their way to the try line, before Ben Earl conceded a yellow card and a penalty try for collapsing.

Saracens were again reduced to 14 men later in the second half after Fergus Burke was shown a yellow for a high tackle on Quins winger Rordigo Isgro.

Lapses of concentration also proved costly for the visitors, with Max Malins sauntering over before Smith, coming from behind, knocked the ball out of his hands before the full-back could touch down for a try.

Saracens took some momentum into the second-half, with Theo Dan crashing over from the back of the maul to cut the deficit to 26-10 at half-time.

Joe Shaw's side improved in the second term, but a fumble from Segun proved costly, with Will Porter picking up the loose ball before charging down the field for an impressive solo try.

"You can't afford to come here and make as many errors as we did in the first-half around our roles and understanding what we were trying to do," Shaw told TNT Sports.

"We were off it. We lost the discipline count. All around, it was pretty disappointing."

articles.title: England rugby squad: Chandler Cunningham-South ruled out of three-day training camp as Steve Borthwick names group
articles.summary: Steve Borthwick has named his 36-player squad for England's three-day training camp ahead of the Autumn Nations Series; Chandler Cunningham-South and Benhard Janse van Rensburg both miss out due to injury
articles.body:
Head coach Steve Borthwick named his 36-player squad for a three-day training camp on Sunday. The team is due to gather at England's Performance Centre at Pennyhill Park later today.

Uncapped forward Kepueli Tuipulotu and scrum-half Archie McParland have both been named in the squad.

Harlequins prop Fin Baxter also returns to the England squad following a 10-month injury lay-off.

Sale Sharks' Joe Marchant has also received a call-up for the first time since the 2023 World Cup after the winger returned to the Gallagher Prem following a two-year stint with Top 14 side Stade Francais at the start of the 2026-27 season.

Seb Atkinson, Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Guy Pepper were all included in the squad and were listed as being in injury rehabilitation.

England will face Australia at Allianz Stadium on Sunday, November 8, before taking on Japan on November 14 and New Zealand on November 21.

articles.title: The Prem: Harlequins 33-15 Saracens - Marcus Smith stars as Quins pick up first win in derby
articles.summary: Marcus Smith sets the tone on his 200th Quins appearance as the Prem's bottom club topple London rivals Saracens 33-15.
articles.body:
Tries: Smith, Driscoll, penalty try, Murley, Porter Cons: Smith (3)

A Marcus Smith-inspired Harlequins registered their first Prem victory of the season with a convincing win over ill-disciplined Saracens in the London derby at The Stoop.

Smith shone throughout and marked his 200th Quins appearance with the opening score as Seb Driscoll, a penalty try and Cadan Murley's ninth London derby try secured rock-bottom Quins a bonus point before half-time.

Sarries stayed in touch with tries from Rotimi Segun and Theo Dan before the turnaround, but two yellow cards made their task harder.

The second half was a tighter affair but Quins extended their lead through Will Porter and despite Nick Tompkins' consolation score, the hosts recorded a third straight home Prem win over their rivals, who could have gone second with victory.

Quins stay bottom but are now only one point behind Exeter and Newcastle with Saracens in fifth, five points behind early leaders Gloucester.

England fly-half Smith set the tone inside three minutes, darting through after some quick handling down the left flank and then converting his own try.

Saracens gave up a series of penalties in the opening stages, allowing Quins to pile on the pressure, and Driscoll burst through Tomos Williams for the second score after 15 minutes following a bulldozing run and quick pass from England prop Fin Baxter, who was making his first start in 10 months after recovering from a foot injury.

The visitors pulled one back four minutes later when Segun jinked to the line in the corner after a quick pass from Max Malins, but Quins were undeterred and were awarded a penalty try on 24 minutes when a rolling maul from a line-out was dragged down on the line, with Ben Earl shown a yellow card.

Sarries thought they had closed the gap further when Malins scampered over the line after Segun brilliantly kept the ball in play, but Smith stole in from behind to slap the ball away before the unsuspecting Malins could ground it.

Moments after Earl returned to the fray, Fergus Burke was sin-binned for a head-to-head tackle on Quins' Rodrigo Isgro as he surged towards the line.

The hosts made Sarries pay within 60 seconds as Murley gathered a long pass on the left flank and dived into the corner.

Saracens did reduce the arrears with the final play of the half, Theo Dan touching down following a rolling maul from his line-out.

Burke was not allowed to return from the bin after failing a head injury assessment, with Angus Hall coming on in his place and Malins switching to fly-half before Sarries made five changes in the pack just seven minutes into the second half.

Porter pounced on a drop from Segun and then strong-armed his way to the line to extend the lead on 55 minutes, with Smith slotting the extras.

Tompkins bounced his way over after a maul on 62 minutes to reduce the arrears but Hall hooked his conversion attempt wide and Sarries were unable to conjure a late bonus point in the face of some solid Quins defence.

"Danny Care is the quintessential Harlequin but I think Marcus [Smith] is number two because of the work that he puts in and the care that he's got for the club.

"He's only 27 years old and has played 200 games for us. We're so lucky to have him and we're so proud of him.

"Everyone knows Harlequins – when we're at our best, we can play a really free-flowing style of rugby, but we've got to have grit on the other side of the ball as well.

"If Marcus isn't going to die on plays, then we're in the contest. That was a really big statement against Max Malins that he set for our boys."

On the return of Fin Baxter and a potential England recall:

"I'd certainly back him after the way he came back. He showed his quality right from the get go.

"We'll bang another game into him against a big Exeter pack next weekend. Hopefully we can push him to 50 minutes, 60 minutes then.

"Whether he comes off the bench or starts, that's up to [England head coach] Steve Borthwick.

"We just don't want to be too greedy with Fin because we haven't had him for a while. He came back and played a really strong game.

"We've just got to make sure we don't overload him too much too early because he's such a good player."

articles.title: Joe Marchant recalled to England set-up by head coach Steve Borthwick
articles.summary: Joe Marchant is recalled to the England set-up after being included in a 36-player training camp for this autumn's Nations Championship matches.
articles.body:
Joe Marchant is back in the England set-up after being included in a 36-player training camp for this autumn's Nations Championship matches.

The 30-year-old centre has not played for England since the 2023 World Cup as he became ineligible after joining Stade Francais and being based in France following the tournament.

However, he became available to Borthwick again having returned to England to play for Sale Sharks and is part of a training squad which assembled on Sunday for a three-day camp.

Marchant, who helped Harlequins become domestic champions in 2021, has earned 26 caps for England.

In September, he made it clear he has ongoing ambitions in the international game, saying: "I want to play for England, that's what I want to do. I'm proud to have played for England and I don't want it to be my last time at that World Cup. I want to play again."

England play Australia on 8 November before facing Japan on 14 November and New Zealand on 21 November.

Former England captain Courtney Lawes is also at Sale Sharks after leaving French side Brive but has not been recalled by Borthwick.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England switch focus to winner-takes-all clash with Samoa after being 'blown away' by Australia
articles.summary: England need to beat Samoa in their final group game to qualify for the Women's Rugby League World Cup semi-finals; England thrashed Wales in their tournament opener before losing 78-0 to Australia on Saturday
articles.body:
Nineteen months on from a humbling 90-4 loss to Australia in Las Vegas, England suffered another heavy defeat against the same opposition after the Jillaroos ran in 15 tries during a one-sided contest.

England now travel from Perth to Wollongong for Friday's winner-takes-all clash with Samoa (6.45am GMT), where a victory is required to finish second in Group A and reach the knockout stages.

"There are some people in the group who were at Vegas and they're in the changing room saying 'this wasn't like Vegas, it doesn't feel like Vegas, you're not part of what happened at Vegas - this is different'," Barrow told reporters.

"Yeah, we didn't help ourselves and the scoreline's still big, but I think people have still got some positivity in there and people don't want to go home. They want to have this game against Samoa and give our best."

Barrow added: "We had to change the way we were going as a group [after Vegas] and we made a lot of changes to bring a young group in. This young group is going to develop and keep developing, and that's a good learning curve from tonight."

Jaime Chapman scored two tries in the opening six minutes for Australia, who were already 36-0 up at half-time, although Barrow was pleased with the commitment of his young England side.

"I thought we fought really well for the whole 70 minutes, and that may sound a little bit silly when you've conceded that many points, but it felt different," Barrow explained. "I thought we competed, but we got beat by a far better team with just too much quality.

"It's really disappointing when you see a score like that. You can't be happy with it in any way, shape or form, but it felt different. It felt like we competed a lot more on plays.

"I don't think we give up, I thought we just kept trying, but once they get a roll on like that, I don't think any team in the world can compete with them. They're just too quick, they're too skilful, and they're too fast for our girls at that stage."

England had started the tournament strongly and showed encouraging signs during their 70-6 win over Wales, with Burrow keen to take attributes from that victory into the must-win Samoa clash.

"We've talked in there (changing room) about what we've been doing really well in training and what we did in patches last week against Wales - we can't forget that because of this (loss), we've got to remember some of that stuff," Burrow insisted.

"I think it was important that we talked in there about our effort areas and how we continue to turn up for each other, and that's going to stand us in good stead in the future.

"Listen, we got blown away by an excellent team. A team I think is, probably, one of the best sporting teams in the world across all sports at the moment. They're dominant and you want to go in there and you want to compete with them.

"We tried at certain areas, but eventually they were just too good and too strong. We've got to stick to our processes, get back on the horse and get ready for another game next week."

England play Samoa in their final pool fixture on Friday (6.45am), where victory in Wollongong will secure a semi-final place. The winner will then play the team finishing top of Pool B in the opening semi-final, taking place in Newcastle on November 7.
